chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
title: The 1944 recording ban and studio pay
summary: The Petrillo strike kept them from recording; studio pay was thirty dollars for four numbers on two tracks.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: ... that it come out different. Well, that's true. All right, in 1944 did you have any problems that you can remember about now?
I noticed you weren't recording then. Is there a reason why you weren't recording?

Well, there was a strike of recording, some kind of problem with the Union. Petrillo, he wants more money for the musicians, which I thought that was right. The company that was making lot of money, paying nothing, no royalty for the musicians, so he considered that we should make more money. Those days, I think, we were making thirty dollars for a session of four numbers.
... in the studio. I see. How long would it take the four numbers to record?

Well, always recording is a very special thing, depend the quality of the musicians. If you had a good musician, you could record in four numbers, you could record in one hour and a half. Give it and take.
In those days there was two tracks.
